Unsupported operator: except. Supply an: The SQL translator has no two-list difference value; the walk refuses except in each arrival position.
Unsupported operator: matches. Supply an: ActiveRecord has no portable RE2 predicate; matches is refused even inside equality or disjunction.
The adapter has no RE2-compatible matches operator across its SQL dialects; the walk refuses matches before emitting SQL.
Unsupported operator: index. Supply an o: Relational associations do not expose CEL positional scalar-list indexing; the adapter refuses index before building a query.

Positional access into a list of numbers, the same refusal as index-scalar-list: `index` has no case in the translator's operator dispatch, so the walk falls through to the generic unsupported-operator refusal before the comparison around it is built. `aNumberList` is a has_many association mapped by member field, and a relation mapping carries no element order, so `aNumberList[0]` names whichever row the engine returns first without an ORDER BY the plan does not carry. A caller whose element table has a position column, as the harness table does, can supply the override the message offers

A caller whose element table has a position column, as the harness table does, can supply the override the message offers

The cross-type probe `aBoolList[0] == 1 || aNumber == 5`, refused at the `index` in its first disjunct for the same missing element order as index-bool-list, so nothing is emitted for either disjunct. The refusal is also what keeps the cross-type hazard shut on this store: SQLite holds a boolean column as the integer 1, so a positional lowering that compared the stored `aBoolList` element with the literal would return b4 and c1, whose first element is true, where CEL's heterogeneous equality is false for every row

The cross-type probe `aNumberList[0] == true || aNumber == 5`, refused at the `index` in its first disjunct for the same missing element order as index-number-list, so nothing is emitted for either disjunct. The refusal is also what keeps the cross-type hazard shut on this store: SQLite reads the literal TRUE as the integer 1, so a positional lowering that compared the stored `aNumberList` element with the literal would return b4, whose first element is 1, where CEL's heterogeneous equality is false for every row
int() applied to a :string column: CEL r: SQL numeric casts accept malformed string prefixes or coerce them to zero, unlike CEL errors; negation cannot make the conversion safe.
timestamp() applied to a :string column:: The mapper supplies a string column; the adapter only compares instants through native temporal columns, without portable error-preserving parsing of malformed strings.
double() needs a numeric column. CEL mak: SQL floating-point casts accept malformed string prefixes or coerce them to zero, unlike CEL errors; negation cannot make the conversion safe.

Cannot divide by a column that may be ze: The inner divisor is a column that may be zero; SQL cannot preserve the IEEE signed-zero infinity needed to evaluate the nested division.
Raw temporal column comparison loses RFC: SQL temporal columns preserve instants but discard the RFC-3339 spelling compared by bare CEL attributes; timestamp wrappers are required.
eq cannot take a collection operand (a r: A relational collection is not a scalar SQL comparison operand; the adapter refuses whole-list equality rather than compare a member.
ne cannot take a collection operand (a r: A relational collection is not a scalar SQL comparison operand; the adapter refuses whole-list equality rather than compare a member.
in requires scalar elements; SQL scalar: SQL scalar membership cannot bind or compare a nested list element; the adapter refuses before constructing the query.
carries sub-microsecond precision, which: The planner folds `now() - duration("24h")` to a literal with nanosecond precision, and ActiveRecord binds a Time into SQL at microsecond precision at best — SQLite stores a formatted string and MySQL DATETIME(6) truncates. Rounding the literal compares against a different instant than the policy names, in the direction that admits rows just outside the window, so the adapter refuses rather than move the boundary
The same sub-microsecond now() literal as ts-window, reached with the operands the other way round. Operand order does not change what a Time binds as, so the refusal is the same one
Cannot divide by a column that may be ze: The denominator is a DIFFERENT column, so it may be zero on a row where the numerator is not. CEL divides to a signed Infinity and IEEE-754 keeps the sign of the zero; SQL cannot tell -0.0 from 0.0, and a NULLIF guard collapses both to NULL. The sign of the Infinity decides which side of an order comparison the row falls on, so no guard recovers it and the adapter refuses. A constant denominator, or a column divided by itself, stays translatable
add cannot take an operand that may be N: CEL carries a NaN or a signed Infinity out of the division and through the arithmetic composed on top of it; SQL has no value that does, because the NULLIF divide-by-zero guard turns the whole sum into NULL. The adapter resolves a non-finite division only where the division IS the comparison operand, so a division nested under further arithmetic fails closed instead of emitting the under-granting filter
The same nested-division limitation as cr-div-then-add, and the arm that proves it matters: `NaN != 2.0` is TRUE and the PDP allows the zero row, while `NULL + 1 <> 2` is UNKNOWN and drops it
Unsupported operator: index: Positional access into a scalar list. `index` has no case in the translator's operator dispatch at all, so the walk falls through to the generic unsupported-operator refusal rather than to a leaf-operand guard — which is why the message names the operator and offers an override. No case was written because row order in a SQL relation is not defined without an ORDER BY the plan does not carry: `tagNames` is a has_many association, and `tagNames[0]` names whichever row the engine happens to return first. A caller whose table has a deterministic ordering column can express it faithfully, and the override the message offers is that escape hatch
eq cannot take a collection operand (a p: map() is held as a projected relation until size() or hasIntersection() gives it a scalar meaning as an aggregate or an EXISTS subquery. Comparing the ordered projection itself to a literal list gives it neither, and a correlated subquery has no ordering to compare element-wise against, so the held projection reaches a plain value position and is refused there
hierarchy() delimiter must be a non-empt: An empty delimiter is refused when the hierarchy operand is parsed, before the descendant LIKE is built: the adapter emits `prefix + delimiter + '%'`, which with an empty delimiter is a bare string-prefix LIKE that also matches the path itself (a2, never its own descendant)

refuses.cast-not-double: double() needs a numeric column. CEL makes an error for a string that is not a number, and Cerbos denies the row, but SQL gives 0.0 and the filter would keep it. Compare the column directly, or give an operator override.
refuses.cast-not-int: int() applied to a :string column: CEL reads the WHOLE string or makes an error, and Cerbos then denies the row, but SQL reads the digits at the front and gives a number, so the filter would keep the row. Compare the column directly, or give an operator override.
refuses.cast-not-timestamp: timestamp() applied to a :string column: this adapter compares instants using the database's own temporal type, so the attribute must map to a datetime column rather than to a column holding a formatted timestamp string
